title: Chapter 72 — The Monkey-Rope
paragraphs: In the tumultuous business of cutting-in and attending to a whale, there is much running back and forth among the crew. Now hands are wanted here, then again hands are wanted there. There is no staying in any one place. At one and the same time everything has to be done everywhere. It is a complicated affair. Now, by reason of the rolling of the ship during these operations, you might easily be tossed overboard — and then the sharks! To guard against such a disaster, monkey-ropes were contrived. At the time of my telling this, Queequeg was working on the whale's vast side, secured to the ship above by a monkey-rope attached to a stout belt around his waist. The other end of this rope was also fastened to a belt around my own waist, so that for better or worse, Queequeg and I were joined.

Being the harpooner's bowsman — that is, the person who pulled the bow-oar in his boat, the second one from forward — it was my cheerful duty to attend upon him while he took that hard-scrabble scramble upon the dead whale's back. You have seen Italian organ-grinders holding a dancing monkey by a long cord. Just so, from the ship's deck, I held Queequeg down there in the sea, by what is technically called in the fishery a monkey-rope, attached to a strong belt around his body.

It was a humorously perilous business for both of us. For before we go further, it must be said that the monkey-rope was fast at both ends — fast to Queequeg's broad canvas belt and fast to my narrow leather one. So that for better or worse, we two, for the time, were wedded. And should poor Queequeg sink to rise no more, then both usage and honor demanded that instead of cutting the cord, it should drag me down in his wake.

So strongly and metaphysically did I feel my situation then, that while earnestly watching his motions, I seemed clearly to perceive that my own individuality was now merged in a joint stock company of two. My free will had received a mortal wound. Another's mistake or misfortune could pull me into unmerited disaster and death. And yet still further, I could see that this particular situation of mine was only the extreme illustration of the general truth — that for the mass of men, the choice of their daily acts is not at all with themselves. All the while, other people's acts are fatally involved with theirs.

The monkey-rope is found in all whalers, but it was only in the Pequod that the monkey and his holder were ever tied together. This improvement upon the original usage was introduced by no less a man than Stubb, in order to afford the imperiled harpooner the strongest possible guarantee for the faithfulness and vigilance of his holder.

I have hinted that I would often jerk poor Queequeg from between the whale and the ship — where he would occasionally fall, from the incessant rolling and swaying of both. But this was not the only danger he was exposed to. Unperturbed by the massacre inflicted on them during the night, the sharks were back again in full force, hungrily snapping at the strips of blubber.

And right in among those sharks was Queequeg, who often pushed them aside with his floundering feet. A thing altogether incredible were it not that, attracted by such prey as a dead whale, the otherwise indiscriminately carnivorous shark will seldom touch a man.

Nevertheless, it may well be believed that since they have such a greedy hand in the pie, it is considered wise to keep a sharp eye on them. Accordingly, besides the monkey-rope, with which I now and then jerked the poor fellow from too close an approach to the jaws of the sharks, Queequeg was further protected by his harpooner friends on deck, who, with long whaling-spades, kept slashing at the nearest sharks. But still the danger was great, for you had to be careful not to strike Queequeg himself.

Well, well, my dear companion and twin-brother, thought I, as I drew in and then slacked off the rope with every swell of the sea — what does it matter, after all? Are you not the precious image of each and all of us men in this whaling world? That unfathomed ocean you gasp in, is Life. Those sharks, your enemies. Those spades, your friends. And what between sharks and spades you are in a sorry fix, and might well feel nervous about it.

But courage! There is good cheer in store for you, Queequeg. For now, as with blue lips and bloodshot eyes the exhausted savage at last climbs up the chains and stands all dripping and involuntarily trembling on the side, the steward advances, and with a kind, consoling glance hands him — what? Some hot cognac? No! Ginger and water!

"Ginger? Do I smell ginger?" suspiciously asked Stubb, coming near. "Yes, this must be ginger," peering into the as yet untasted cup. Then standing as if incredulous for a while, he calmly walked toward the astonished steward and slowly said, "Ginger? Ginger? And will you have the goodness to tell me, Mr. Dough-Boy, where you got this ginger?"

"There is some sneaking Temperance Society movement about this business," he suddenly added, now approaching Starbuck, who had just come from forward. "Will you look at that cup, sir — smell of it, if you please." Then watching the mate's face, he added, "The steward, Mr. Starbuck, had the audacity to offer ginger-water to Queequeg after that dangerous work!"
"I trust not," said Starbuck. "It is poor stuff enough."

"Aye, aye, steward," cried Stubb. "We'll teach you to drug a harpooner! None of your apothecary's medicine here! You want to poison us, do you? You've got life insurance on us and want to murder us all and pocket the money, do you?"
"It was not me," cried Dough-Boy. "It was Aunt Charity that brought the ginger on board, and told me never to give the harpooners any spirits, but only this ginger-jub — so she called it."
"Ginger-jub! You gingery rascal! Take that! And run along to the lockers and get something better. I hope I do no wrong, Mr. Starbuck. It is the captain's orders — grog for the harpooner on a whale."
"Enough," replied Starbuck. "Only don't hit him again, but —"
"Oh, I never hurt when I hit, except when I hit a whale or something of that sort. And this fellow's a weasel. What were you about saying, sir?"
"Only this: go down with him, and get what you want yourself."

When Stubb reappeared, he came with a dark flask in one hand and a sort of tea-caddy in the other. The first contained strong spirits and was handed to Queequeg. The second was Aunt Charity's gift, and that was freely given to the waves.
